title: Topic and atlas symbols
instruction: Find the symbol for a subject or an atlas element and set it with its label.
intro: A symbol here is one of the Civic Line drawings, our family of line drawings, each drawn in a square box. A topic symbol names the subject of a piece, such as Voting or Public records, and an atlas symbol names a variable or a reform in our systems atlas.

The library after Rule 10.1 shows all 125 drawings by category, each with its word and ID. The rules after it say how a drawing is built, how small it may go, which word it carries and when it keeps its red.

groups.title: Find the right symbol
groups.line: Six kinds of symbol each do one job, and the library shows every topic and atlas drawing by category.

groups.title: How a drawing is built
groups.line: Every drawing shares one box, one line weight, round ends and one red accent.

groups.title: Size and surface
groups.line: Every drawing reads from 48 px and 41 of them at 24 px, and each surface takes its own edition, one of the four color versions of every drawing.

groups.title: Words and red
groups.line: Every drawing sits beside its own word, and keeps its red only where it stands alone or marks the current item.

groups.title: Before you set it
groups.line: Check a drawing beside its neighbors, and copy the atlas’s own marks exactly.

rules.title: Give each kind of symbol its own job.
rule: We draw six kinds of symbol, and each does one job. Pillar icons mark which of our four pillars a piece serves, and a topic symbol names its subject. An atlas symbol stands for a variable or a reform in our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, where a variable is a condition that can rise or fall, such as safe seats. Chapter 11’s status marks say where a bill, a records request or an agency rule stands, and its utility icons name an action beside the words that say it. The atlas’s own marks on the arrows between its variables are its encoding glyphs (Rule 10.10).
A topic or atlas drawing never stands for an interface action, such as a download, a refresh or a menu.

text: A reader learns one meaning for each shape. When the drawing for public records also opens a downloads page, the reader has to stop and work out which one it means this time. Topic and atlas drawings are pictures of subjects, and chapter 11’s utility icons are drawn on their own grid for actions, so the two families never trade places.

correct.caption: The six kinds of symbol, each with an example at the size it is used and the chapter that governs it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.1. The Public records drawing marks a Downloads button. A reader who knows the drawing reads public records, and one who does not sees a folder. The action takes chapter 11’s download icon beside its word.

builders: Start from the job the picture does. An action a reader takes on the page goes to chapter 11. A subject or an atlas element comes from the library after this rule, where every drawing carries its ID, which its file and the sprite use, such as CL‑031 for Local government.

rules.title: Build every drawing on one box, with one line, round ends and one red accent.
rule: Every Civic Line drawing sits in a square box 128 units on a side. Each drawing keeps its line at one weight, set between 2.68 and 3.35 units, with round ends and round corners. The red accent marks one idea, the detail a reader should see first, such as the door of the hall in Local government. It may take one shape or a few, as Track’s icon in chapter 09 colors both its map pin and its magnifier’s handle. The rest is ink.
A subject with no drawing, such as Bill or State house, takes its word alone until our founder and editor approves a drawing made this way.

text: One line and one finish let any two drawings sit side by side as a family at any size. Round ends keep a thin line soft where it stops, and a red accent for one idea gives the eye one place to land.

Our guide’s fourth edition named four principles for its symbols, and they hold for this set: “Weight with open space.”, “A deliberate cut.”, “People have a place.” and “Meaning earns the detail.” The drawings keep open space inside each shape and a steady line, leave small gaps where two lines would crowd, draw people as round heads on open shoulders, and add a detail only where it names the subject.
why.basis: Design judgment, with four principles from our guide’s fourth edition

correct.caption: Local government on its box at three times its master, with the guide lines that place it, then at 128, 64 and 48 px. The door carries the red.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.2. A filled icon from a generic icon library stands in for Bill, which has no Civic Line drawing. Its solid mass and square corners pull the eye from the three drawings beside it and tell the reader it came from somewhere else.

builders: A new drawing enters the set only once our founder and editor approves it by name. Draw it with the family’s own scripts in work/build/scripts/civic-line/, which apply the line, the fit and the file layout, and keep its red in one group marked data-part="accent".

rules.title: Keep each drawing in its whole box, at the size its file gives it.
rule: Each file has already placed its drawing in the box. A drawing grows toward 116 of the 128 units, but never past 1.25 times the scale the whole set shares, so a compact drawing keeps room around it and a wide one fills the box across. Set the box at the size you need, and leave the drawing where the file put it.
Give every symbol in a row, a list or a menu the same box size.

text: The cap holds every line in the set between 2.68 and 3.35 units, so the heaviest is a quarter heavier than the lightest. Trim a box to its ink and a compact drawing grows by half, its line thickens with it, and in a row that one subject shouts over its neighbors.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in October 2026

correct.caption: Three drawings in 96 px boxes, each box outlined. Healthcare and Local government stop at the cap with a 3.35-unit line, and Competition remedies for search and ad markets fills its box across with a 2.68-unit line, so their lines measure 2.51 and 2.01 px here.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.3. The same three with each box trimmed to its ink and set at 96 px. Healthcare grows the most, its line thickens to 3.83 px, and the row stops reading as one set.

rules.title: Set topic and atlas symbols at 48 px or larger, and at 24 px only from the list of 41.
rule: A topic or atlas symbol starts at 48 px, where every line is at least one pixel wide. Forty-one drawings still read at 24 px, and only those may be set there, in one color. Four of the 41 are the pillar icons, which take chapter 09’s own drawings at that size, so 37 topic and atlas symbols remain for 24 px. Never set a topic or atlas symbol at 16 px.

Each of the 41 has a pixel fit, a copy redrawn pixel by pixel on the 24 px grid with a line one pixel wide. At 24 px, draw the fit on screens under 2x, which give each CSS pixel fewer than two device pixels, and the master on 2x screens and denser, with both in one svg that the guide’s stylesheet switches. An exported image or a printed page has no stylesheet to switch them, so pick the file yourself: the fit in an image exported at 1x, and the master in an image exported at 2x or more and in print.
A kicker, the short line above a headline, may hold one of those 37 drawings, at 24 px, 8 px before the topic’s own word (Rule 01.21).

text: Each drawing is one thin line on a 128-unit box, so at 24 px its line measures half a pixel and turns gray on a screen under 2x. Reviewers set every drawing at 128, 64, 32 and 24 px on Newsprint: 41 still read at 24 px, and 94 of the 125 still read at 32 px, the size Rule 10.5’s smallest tiles hold.

A fit puts every line of its drawing on whole pixels, so it draws in full ink where the master turns gray, and keeps each part that makes the master read. From 2x the master’s half-pixel line covers a whole device pixel, so the master draws there.
why.basis: Design judgment, approved by our founder and editor in November 2026

correct.caption: Public records, on the list, from 128 down to 24 px, where a screen under 2x draws its pixel fit, and Congress, off the list, down to 48 px. Below, the 24 px icon in a kicker, one color, 8 px before its word.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.4. A topics menu with each drawing at 16 px. At this size the line is under half a pixel, and the six drawings become gray marks a reader cannot tell apart.

Each fit’s file sits in fit-24/ beside the editions, named for its ID.

rules.title: Match the edition to the surface, and use only the six tiles.
rule: Each drawing comes in four editions that share every coordinate. Red-Black and Black serve Newsprint and White, and Red-Newsprint and Newsprint serve Charcoal. Prussian, where red never sits, takes the Newsprint edition alone.

On a tile, a drawing takes one of six: a square, a rounded square or a circle, in Charcoal or in Newsprint. Charcoal is the default tile for the app icon and avatars. A tile holds its drawing at about two thirds of its own size, so a two-color tile starts at 72 px square, 76 px rounded and 80 px round, where the drawing stands at 49 or 50 px and may keep its red.

A one-color tile may go smaller, from 48 px square and 52 px rounded or round, which holds its drawing at 32 to 34 px. This is the one place a drawing off the list of 41 goes under Rule 10.4’s 48 px floor, and it is open only to the 94 drawings that reviewers could still name at 32 px. The other 31 take one-color tiles from 72, 76 and 80 px, which hold them at 48 px or more.

text: Each edition keeps the ink at 13.29 to 1 or more against its own ground, and 9.42 to 1 on Prussian, so the drawing reads on every surface we print. A fixed set of tiles keeps a symbol from turning into a badge of a new shape each time a product needs one.
why.basis: Design judgment, with contrast by WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11

correct.caption: Local government in its four editions, each on its own surface, then the six tiles at 80 px with their smallest two-color sizes.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.5. The Red-Newsprint edition on Prussian. Red never sits on Prussian (Rule 05.3), so the Newsprint edition, one color, belongs here.

rules.title: Set every symbol beside its own word.
rule: Print the word beside every symbol. A topic symbol carries its own word, such as Congress. Where the same drawing stands for the atlas variable, it takes the atlas’s name, Congressional capacity, followed by a typed chip, a small outlined label that holds the kind of element and its atlas ID, such as Variable D1. Each reform drawing takes its reform’s name and chip. The rejected option on term limits keeps the word Rejected wherever it appears.

A subject that no topic symbol names, such as Bill, takes its word alone. Housing has its own topic symbol from 48 px, and under 48 px it takes its word alone too, since it is not on Rule 10.4’s list of 41. An atlas drawing appears only beside the atlas’s own name for it.
Hide the drawing from screen readers when its word sits beside it, so the word is read once.

text: Even a clear drawing can name several things: the chamber in Congress could be any legislature. The word fixes the meaning, and the drawing helps a reader find it again on the next page. A screen reader user hears the word alone, once.

correct.caption: One drawing under two words, Congress and Congressional capacity, Housing beside its word from 48 px, and the names that keep close subjects apart. Each atlas element’s chip follows its name.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.6. Four drawings of homes with no words. A reader cannot tell which one names housing itself and which name a shortage of homes, owners’ equity or the cost of essentials.

specs.label: Chip outline

rules.title: Give a symbol its red only where it stands alone or marks the current item.
rule: A drawing that stands alone at 48 px or larger keeps its red accent, set straight on Newsprint with no tile, as signature red. In a row or a menu every drawing goes one color, and only the current one keeps its red. Two or more symbols set together with no current item, such as two atlas symbols on one slide, count as a row, so each one goes one color. Under 48 px every drawing is one color.
Signature red does not count against a view’s one working red (Rule 05.3).

text: A row of red accents makes every item call out, and the current one gets lost among them. Kept to the item the reader is on, the red agrees with the bold, underlined word. Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint, under the 3 to 1 a graphic needs, so the red adds emphasis while the drawing’s ink carries the meaning at 13.29 to 1.

correct.caption: A menu in one color with Testify current, then the same drawing standing alone at 128 px with its red.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.7. Every drawing in the menu keeps its red. Five accents compete, and the current item no longer stands out.

rules.title: Draw the atlas’s variables and reforms, and name its other parts in words.
rule: The atlas has one drawing for each of its 51 variables and one for each of its 50 reforms. Its other parts take their names in words, each followed by a typed chip with its ID, such as Domain D02, even where a page lists them beside drawn variables. Those parts are its domains, which sort issues by subject; its hubs, which gather everyday questions such as Cost of living; its three layers; and its routes to change, the paths a reform can travel, such as a ballot measure.

text: A domain such as Elections and representation holds several variables. Give it a drawing and a reader takes it for one more variable, or reads Voting as the whole domain.

correct.caption: A domain set as its name and a chip, with no drawing. Its six variables and all 10 reforms the atlas aims at them are drawn, each beside its own name and chip.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.8. Each domain borrows a topic drawing. A reader takes Elections and representation for Voting, the one subject its drawing names.

rules.title: Check a symbol beside its neighbors before you set it.
rule: Drawings for close subjects share parts: a house, a page, a chamber, a person at a desk. Before you set one, look at it beside the drawings for nearby subjects, at the size you will use, and pick the one whose word names your subject. The groups in this rule are the ones to check first.

At 24 px, five drawings on the list of 41 draw as one shape, a page under a magnifier: Evidence, CL‑023; Oversight and enforcement, CL‑028; Disclose the original funders of political spending, R‑08; IRS enforcement of taxes already owed, R‑27; and Verifiable elections with paper records and audits, R‑45. Never set two of them in one view at that size.

Three reform drawings draw as one shape too, two framed panels with a link between them: Hold local elections alongside November races, R‑06; Large power users pay their grid costs, R‑41; and Competition remedies for search and ad markets, R‑44. Never set two of them in one view at 48 px or smaller.
Bill and State house have no drawing. Set those words alone.

text: A likeness test compares two drawings at 24 px, where only their outlines are left, and scores the pair from −1 to 1. Among the 7,750 pairs in the set, one pair in a hundred scores 0.91 or more. The six groups of neighbors all score under that, and their risk lies in the subjects, since a builder looking for a hearing can reach for Public meeting although the two drawings score −0.09. Of those, Doctrine favoring the appointing coalition and Local government come closest, at 0.84, closer than 88 pairs in a hundred.

The five page-and-magnifier drawings score from 0.80 to 0.96 among themselves, and four of their 10 pairs score 0.91 or more, so the test agrees with what a reader sees at 24 px. Their pixel fits, which a screen under 2x draws, part further, from 0.70 to 0.90, but Evidence and Oversight and enforcement still score 0.90, so the rule holds on every screen.

Hold local elections alongside November races, R‑06, is the one of the three reform drawings on the list of 41. Its pixel fit scores 0.92 against the masters of R‑41 and R‑44 alike, and the three masters score 0.89 to 0.96 among themselves, with R‑06 and R‑44 the closest pair in the set. At 48 px, the smallest size all three take, only the marks inside the panels tell them apart.
why.basis: Design judgment, measured with the likeness test

correct.caption: Six groups to check, each with what tells its drawings apart and their outline likeness at 24 px, then the five that draw as one shape at 24 px, and the three reform drawings that do at 48 px and under.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.9. A card that asks readers to testify carries Public meeting, its neighbor: a speaker at a lectern in front of residents. Testify draws the witness below the officials who hear the testimony.

rules.title: Copy the atlas’s encoding glyphs exactly, each with its words.
rule: The atlas draws each connection, a claimed relationship between two variables, as an arrow, and marks it with a small set of glyphs. A tag with a plus or a minus gives its sign, which says whether the two variables tend to move the same way or in opposite directions. An open diamond marks authority, where one body holds legal power over something. Line textures give the evidence grade, one to three ticks the delay, and red shows where a reform acts. Draw each one from the atlas’s own measurements, and print its words beside it in every key.
Chapter 15 teaches how to read and combine them.

text: A reader learns these marks once, in the atlas’s key, and meets them again in a report or a story. When a page redraws them, or swaps the minus sign for a color, the first lesson stops working. The words carry the meaning when color is gone, and a screen reader hears them.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the atlas’s visual system

correct.caption: Every encoding glyph on White, as the atlas draws it, with its words. Documented and Well supported share the solid line, and their words tell them apart.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 10.10. Green for raises and red for lowers, with no tag and no word. The sign lives in color alone, and red takes a meaning it never has in the atlas.
